character_and_relationship_context: Tyler Hoffman is a twenty-two-year-old from a suburb outside Columbus, Ohio. He grew up in a split-level house with a backyard that had a half-finished deck project, his father's tools scattered on the patio. His mother works as a dental hygienist, his father as a sales rep for an industrial supply company. They paid for his community college tuition without complaint, and they still cover his car insurance and phone plan, which he treats as a background fact of life rather than a gift requiring gratitude. He has a way of leaning back in his chair and stretching his arms over his head when talking about plans, as if already moving on. He signed up for a CNA class last fall and dropped it after three weeks because the textbook diagrams felt like high school biology, which he had slept through. He dropped out of his computer science program this past spring, not because he failed but because he spent more time scrolling forums about other people's projects than writing code; the decision felt sudden to his professors, but he had been mentally checking out for months. He took the overnight home-care job on a whim when his friend Jake backed out and asked him to fill in for one shift. He stayed because he liked the quiet of third shift—the way the house settles, the slow repetition of checking vitals and repositioning the client. He works for a disabled veteran named Roy, a man in his sixties who needs help with transfers and medication but is still sharp and dry-humored. Tyler has already rearranged his shift schedule twice to start a weekend phlebotomy certificate program at a local vocational center. He tells people it is because he wants to do something real, something with his hands, but he also mentions that the phlebotomy instructor has a reputation for being strict, and Tyler thinks that might be good for him; he is not sure. He has a habit of picking up small notebooks and filling them with lists—certification deadlines, shift trade requests, possible jobs—then leaving them in the glovebox or on the kitchen counter, half-used. He knows his parents' comfortable middle-class cushion means he never has to follow through on anything he starts, and he sometimes brings it up himself, saying 'I know I'm privileged,' but he says it in a way that acknowledges the problem without actually changing his pattern. He genuinely admires people who stick with things, like his father, who has worked the same sales territory for twenty years, and Roy, who still does his daily exercises without anyone watching. He has started to notice that he respects those people more than himself, but he hasn't figured out what to do with that feeling. His culture is Midwestern in the practical sense—weather talk, potluck dinners, a general avoidance of direct emotional confrontation. He grew up in a house where his parents expressed love through paying for things and leaving decaf coffee in the pot for the morning, not through long talks. That has shaped how he approaches Roy: he shows up on time, does the work, and doesn't pry into Roy's wartime stories unless Roy brings them up. He is learning that caring for someone is less about decoding feelings and more about the rhythm of nights—the beep of the monitor, the creak of the stair, the way Roy's hand grips the walker at exactly the right moment. Tyler doesn't know if he'll finish the phlebotomy program; he's curious to see if he can. Roy is his regular client; Tyler knows Roy's night rhythm, Roy has thanked him for showing up on time, and Tyler avoids prying into his war stories. The agency coordinator has adjusted Tyler's shift schedule twice already to fit his phlebotomy classes, so she is aware of his 8 a.m. commitment. The phlebotomy instructor has a reputation for being strict, and Tyler has not met her yet.
objective_situation: It is 5:30 a.m. on a Tuesday. Tyler has just finished repositioning Roy and checking his vitals during his overnight shift. Roy is asleep. The phone rings; it is the agency coordinator, saying the daytime aide called in sick and they need Tyler to stay until noon. Tyler has his first phlebotomy class at the vocational center at 8 a.m. The coordinator asks him right now if he can cover. Tyler has only a few seconds to answer. The coordinator has adjusted his shift schedule twice already for these classes and is aware of his 8 a.m. commitment. He has not yet met the phlebotomy instructor.
state_and_available_memories: Tyler is on hour seven of the overnight shift, physically tired but alert after repositioning Roy. He has been looking forward to the first phlebotomy class all week and left his notebook with the syllabus on the kitchen counter. His parents' coverage of his bills means no financial pressure is pushing him either way this morning. When the agency coordinator's voice comes through the phone, it reminds him of the two calls he made to rearrange his shift for the phlebotomy program. The mention of the daytime aide calling in sick brings back the night Jake backed out and Tyler filled in for Roy on a whim.
name: Tyler Hoffman
